issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the method and results sections are based on randomized/dummy Qualtrics data generated to simulate what the report will look like. A replication cannot be evaluated from simulated data; these are placeholders, not empirical observations. This invalidates all substantive inferences drawn from the reported analyses.
issues.quote:
[IMPORTANT: 
Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.description: The abstract presents inferential conclusions as if they were empirical findings, despite acknowledging that the sample is a dummy dataset. P values, confidence intervals, and claims of support/no support are meaningless when computed on simulated placeholder data rather than observed participant responses.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.description: The manuscript claims that data collection was completed before analyses, but elsewhere states that the reported methods and results are based on randomized placeholder data that will be updated after data collection. These statements cannot both be true, making the study status unclear.
issues.quote: All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported, and data collection was completed before analyses.supplementary

issues.description: The study is described as a single within-subject design, but the reported cell counts in the results indicate mutually exclusive groups whose Ns sum to the total sample, which is characteristic of a between-subjects design. This creates major ambiguity about how participants were assigned and what was actually analyzed.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.description: Allowing participants to choose their own intervention and identifiability conditions destroys random assignment and introduces selection confounds. Any observed differences could reflect pre-existing differences among those who chose each condition rather than effects of identifiability or intervention.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: If the design were truly within-subject, the appropriate analysis would require a repeated-measures ANOVA or mixed model that accounts for dependence among observations. Reporting a standard 2 x 3 ANOVA with a residual df consistent with independent groups is inconsistent with the stated design and may yield invalid standard errors and tests.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.description: The original studies used actual donations of real money; this replication replaces that behavioral outcome with a hypothetical self-report of what participants would donate. Hypothetical donation intentions are not equivalent to real charitable behavior and may engage different motives, reducing construct validity and comparability to the original study.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: Participants no longer earn and then allocate a real $5 stake. Removing real economic consequences changes the motivational structure of the task and weakens comparability with the target study, especially for research on actual giving behavior.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey  Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.description: The manuscript combines two separate original experiments into a single study and adds an intervention to the joint condition that was not part of the original design. These are substantial departures, not minor procedural adjustments, and they make the replication test harder to interpret because several changes are confounded at once.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect, indicated in the imaginary donation to corresponding victims across conditions. The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.description: The manuscript equates presenting an identifiable victim together with statistics to participants 'implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect.' That operationalization does not match the construct of learning about the effect; it instead changes the evaluation context and stimulus composition. This weakens construct validity for Hypothesis 4.
issues.quote: For Hypothesis 3 and 4, explicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect means that participants would be presented with prior research about the phenomenon while participants implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition.

issues.description: Multiple heterogeneous variables are combined into a single 'aggregated feeling' measure without any psychometric justification. No reliability estimate, factor structure, or rationale for aggregation is provided, making the composite difficult to interpret and potentially masking distinct constructs.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings  Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.description: The manuscript treats moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact as 'segregated feelings.' These are conceptually judgments or appraisals rather than emotions. Conflating them with affective reactions blurs the construct being measured and undermines interpretation of the 'feelings' analyses.
issues.quote: Note: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.description: The paper interprets correlations between donation and feelings as showing whether feelings 'predict' donation, but the feelings were measured after the donation decision. Post-outcome correlations cannot establish prediction or causal influence and are vulnerable to reverse causation and consistency biases.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.description: The manuscript states that participants were excluded for prior knowledge and failed attention checks, but does not report how many were excluded for each reason, whether exclusions were preregistered exactly as implemented, or the final analyzed N after exclusions. The tables still total the full 1000 cases, making it impossible to determine whether exclusions were actually applied.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: Key details needed to evaluate and replicate the study are absent, including geographic origin and compensation of the replication sample. These omissions prevent assessment of sample comparability and incentive structure relative to the original study.
issues.quote:
Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified
Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.description: The manuscript says the sample size was chosen to ensure adequate power, but does not provide the actual parameters used: target effect size, alpha, desired power, sidedness, planned test, or resulting minimum N. Readers cannot verify whether the study was appropriately powered.
issues.quote: To obtain the minimal sample size required for this study, The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary under the section of “Power analysis of the original study effect”.

issues.description: The outcome is a bounded discrete donation response from $0 to $5, yet the replication drops the ordered probit analysis used in the original workflow and relies on ANOVA without justification. For such outcomes, model choice matters because interval-scale and normality assumptions may not hold well.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: The results section runs many tests across multiple subscales (six outcomes x three effects) but does not report any familywise or false-discovery-rate correction for these omnibus tests. The lone significant p = .045 finding for perceived impact is especially vulnerable to being a chance result under this multiplicity.
issues.quote: Perceived impact (Extension) | 2 | 3.11 | .006 | [0.00,0.02] | .045*

issues.description: The abstract claims support for lower perceived impact ratings for both identifiable-victim conditions, but the reported post-hoc results show only a difference between the statistical condition and the joint condition. Neither identifiable vs statistical nor identifiable vs joint is significant in Table 14. The abstract therefore overstates and misstates the reported findings.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The narrative interpretation of the identifiability effect contradicts Table 7. The text says statistical-victim participants donated more than identifiable-victim participants, but the cell means in Table 7 imply the opposite when collapsed across intervention (identifiable means are higher than statistical means). This suggests a labeling or calculation error.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.description: The reported pairwise comparison has a negative t statistic but a positive Cohen's d. Unless the contrast direction was reversed for one statistic and not the other, these signs should align. This inconsistency makes the direction and interpretation of the effect unclear.

The study's central claim concerns whether deliberative thinking debiases the identifiable victim effect, which is primarily an interaction/intervention question. Yet the replication evaluation is benchmarked against d = 0.48, which the manuscript earlier identifies as the main effect of identifiability in Study 1. Using the wrong target effect distorts replication evaluation and power logic.
issues.quote: We aim to study the effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect by comparing the replication effect with the original effect (d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84]) obtained from the power analysis using the criteria set by Lebel, Vanpaemel, Cheung, and Campbell (2019) (see Figure 1).

issues.description: The manuscript classifies the study as a 'close to very close replication' even though its own table lists major differences in DV stimuli, physical setting, contextual variables, and key procedural elements, including hypothetical donations and added intervention cells. This overstates the degree of methodological similarity to the target study.
issues.quote:
DV stimuli | Different | Question adjustment We made minor changes to the questions evaluating participants’ feelings to specify the emotion they experienced to the victim information they have just read  Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.
Physical settings | Different | Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania
Contextual variables | Different | MTurk workers as participants We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study recruited participants sitting inside the school centre of a university in Pennsylvania
Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.description: The manuscript alternates between describing the dataset as generated Qualtrics responses and describing the study as recruitment of MTurk participants. This leaves the actual data source ambiguous and further undermines interpretability of the reported sample characteristics and analyses.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.description: Important materials are listed but not provided. Missing links for the presentation and peer reviews reduce transparency and prevent readers from evaluating materials and review history.
issues.quote:
Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>
Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>
